member.name: T:Sluice.ShmFrameChannel
member.summary:
A bidirectional over two s — one per direction. The server side creates both rings; the client side opens them, swapped, so each side reads what the other writes. This is the drop-in replacement for a duplex NamedPipeStream, but frame-native and zero-copy on read.
One channel is point-to-point. A multiplexing daemon (one process serving many client connections) gives each connection its own uniquely-named channel; pair this with a small accept/rendezvous step so a fresh client and the daemon agree on that name. (That broker is intentionally not baked in here — it belongs to the daemon's connection model.)

member.summary: Connect to a daemon that is running a on . The client mints a unique connection id, creates its per-connection rings, and announces itself on the listener's accept ring; the listener's next picks it up. Returns the client side of a fresh duplex channel.

member.name: T:Sluice.ShmFrameListener
member.summary:
The daemon-side acceptor that turns Sluice's point-to-point into a multiplexed server: many client processes connect, each gets its own duplex channel, and one daemon services them all. This is the Sluice analogue of NamedPipeServerStream.WaitForConnection — the rendezvous a frame-based daemon (e.g. an LSP multiplexer holding one language server) needs.
Protocol: the listener owns a small accept ring. A connecting client mints a unique id, creates its per-connection rings, then posts the id; reads the id, opens those rings, and returns the server side of the channel. Per-connection routing is the application's job (just as it is over named pipes) — the listener only hands you fresh channels.

member.summary: Delivery semantics for a multicast ring.

member.name: F:Sluice.DeliveryMode.Reliable
member.summary: No message is dropped: a producer waits until the slowest registered subscriber has passed the slot it wants to reuse. Correct for commands/events you must not lose (but a stalled subscriber backpressures everyone — use only with well-behaved consumers).

member.name: F:Sluice.DeliveryMode.Lossy
member.summary: A producer never waits on consumers: it overwrites the oldest slot. A subscriber that falls more than a ring behind detects the gap (its slot was overwritten by a newer sequence) and resyncs forward, dropping what it missed. Lowest latency, crash-robust — market-data / telemetry style.

member.name: T:Sluice.ShmMulticast
member.summary:
A many-to-many multicast ring in shared memory — the multi-way core of Sluice. It is a Disruptor-style sequenced ring: producers claim a globally-monotonic sequence with a single interlocked increment, write their slot, then stamp the slot's sequence as the publish barrier. Every subscriber keeps its own cursor and reads every message in place (a span straight into the shared pages). The same per-slot stamp doubles as the lap detector that makes lossy delivery possible.
One producer ⇒ broadcast (1→N). Many producers ⇒ a full bus (N↔N) — the interlocked claim makes multi-producer safe with no lock. Slot count must be a power of two; each slot is fixed size and holds [long sequence][int length][payload…].
Platform: cross-platform via — a named map on Windows, a /dev/shm file-backed map on Linux. The creation-race in is arbitrated by on Windows and by an atomic on Unix.

member.name: T:Sluice.ShmRing
member.summary:
A single-producer / single-consumer (SPSC) lock-free ring buffer that lives entirely inside a memory-mapped file, so it can be shared between two processes on the same machine.
The defining property — and the reason this library exists — is read-in-place: the consumer receives a pointing directly into the shared memory pages. There is no copy out of the ring and no deserialize step on the read path. Contrast this with Cloudtoid.Interprocess, which copies every message body out of the ring into a pooled/allocated buffer before handing it back (it clears the slot and advances the read cursor immediately, so it cannot hand out a stable view). Sluice keeps the slot alive until you call , which is what makes genuine zero-copy possible.
Framing: messages are laid out as [int length][payload…], each frame 4-byte aligned. Cursors are monotonic 64-bit byte counts (never wrapped); the physical position is offset % Capacity. A frame never straddles the wrap boundary — when the tail of the buffer is too small, the producer writes a filler that tells the consumer to jump to the next boundary.
Coordination is via two cursors in a cache-line-separated header plus an optional "doorbell" so the consumer can block instead of spin. The ring itself is correct without the doorbell (you can poll ); the doorbell is purely a latency/CPU trade-off.
Platform: cross-platform. On Windows the shared region is a named (page-file-backed) memory-mapped file with a named doorbell. On Linux/Unix — where named maps and named wait handles are unsupported in .NET — it is a file-backed map under /dev/shm (tmpfs, so still RAM-resident) and the doorbell degrades to polling (the ring is correct without it). Named , used by the discovery and MPSC layers, works on both. This is what lets Sluice run in Azure Container Apps (Linux) as well as on Windows.
